title: Triples with Bitwise AND Equal To Zero
spaceBreakdown:
- vector<int> f of size 65536 (pair-AND counts, reused as SOS table) → O(2^16)
- loop variables → O(1)
- not counted: input nums, returned int
approach: A triple (x, a, b) has AND zero iff a&b is a subset of the complement of x. Count, for every 16-bit mask v, how many ordered pairs (i,j) have nums[i]&nums[j] = v (O(n²)), then run a Sum-Over-Subsets (SOS) DP so f[mask] = number of pairs whose AND is a subset of mask (O(2^16·16)). The answer is the sum over every element x of f[~x & 0xFFFF].
hints:
The values are tiny (< 2^16) but n can be 1000 - instead of asking "which triples work?", ask: if for EVERY 16-bit mask you knew how many pairs of elements AND to something inside that mask, how fast could you finish each element x?
With n = 1000 there are ~10^6 pairs - that part is cheap; the question is what table makes the third element O(1).

Build a count array over all 2^16 masks of pair-AND values, then run a Sum-over-Subsets (SOS) DP so each cell holds the count of pairs whose AND is a subset of that mask. For nums = [2,1,3], pair-AND counts are 0→2, 1→3, 2→3, 3→1; after SOS, f[13] = 5 (pairs with AND ⊆ 13), and element 2 contributes f[~2 & 15] = f[13] = 5 triples.

**Single element, value 0** - n = 1 with nums = [0]; the only triple is (0,0,0).
`Input: [0]` → `Expected: 1`
⚠️ Bug: skipping i==j==k pairs when filling the pair table (requiring distinct indices) → returns 0.

**All equal, nonzero** - every triple ANDs to the same nonzero value.
`Input: [1,1,1]` → `Expected: 0`
⚠️ Bug: counting pairs whose AND is a SUPERSET of ~x instead of a subset → returns 27.

**All zeros** - every pair ANDs to 0, which is a subset of every mask.
`Input: [0,0,0]` → `Expected: 27`
⚠️ Bug: forgetting mask 0 is a subset of every mask in the SOS base case → returns 0.

**Maximum value element** - 65535 has no zero bits, so its complement is 0.
`Input: [65535,1]` → `Expected: 4` (only triples containing the 1 work: 6 orderings minus the two all-65535-heavy ones... precisely the 4 triples with at least one 1)
⚠️ Bug: indexing f[~x] without masking to 16 bits (negative index for values ≥ 2^15 if using signed shift) → out-of-bounds crash.

**Count size** - worst case n = 1000 of zeros gives 1000³ = 10^9 triples.
`Input: [0]*1000` → `Expected: 1000000000`
⚠️ Bug: accumulating in a 16-bit or 8-bit counter during the SOS pass (a cell can hold up to 10^6 pair counts) → wrong counts.

followUps.q: What if values can be up to 2^20 and n up to 10^5?
followUps.a: The pair table of size 2^20 is still feasible, but O(n²) = 10^10 pair enumeration is not; split elements into two halves and meet in the middle, or use the O(n · 2^b) trick of iterating masks per element only when n² < 2^b · b. Time becomes O(min(n², n·2^b) + 2^b·b), space O(2^b).

followUps.q: What if you only need to know WHETHER a triple with AND zero exists, not the count?
followUps.a: Keep the same SOS table but store booleans: mark which pair-AND values occur, propagate subset reachability with SOS, and answer exists iff any x has f[~x] > 0. Time stays O(n² + 2^16·16) but you can early-exit and use bitsets for space O(2^16/8) bytes.

followUps.q: What if the array is given as a stream and you must answer after each new element?
followUps.a: Maintain the pair-count table incrementally: each new element x adds n+1 new pairs (x with each previous element and with itself), an O(n) update, then the SOS layer can also be updated incrementally per new pair in O(16). Per-element cost O(n·16), total O(n²·16), space O(2^16).
